paragraphs.source_en: Tsangyang Gyatso (1683-1745) is a famous figure in Tibetan history. He was born in the place called Lawo Yusong in Monyul; gifted and quick-witted from childhood, he once studied under the Fifth Panchen Lama, shaved his head and received ordination, and took the Dharma name Lobsang Rinchen Tsangyang Gyatso. Later he was welcomed to the Potala Palace, where, under the direct tutelage of the renowned scholar Sangye Gyatso, he studied astronomy and calendrical calculation, medicine, literature, and other subjects, and attained deep accomplishment in poetry. At the age of twenty-five, Tsangyang Gyatso, made a victim of the upper ruling class's struggle for power and profit, began his life of wandering. He traveled in succession through Qinghai, Gansu, Mongolia, Sichuan, U-Tsang, India, Nepal, and other places. He was once a beggar and once carried corpses; his life was extremely hard. Because he came into contact with the broad masses of the people and possessed rich lived experience, he was able to write the beautiful and moving Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso. Another account says that Tsangyang Gyatso was killed while being escorted to Beijing, and that his works were written before the age of twenty-five.

units.source_en: Tsangyang Gyatso (1683-1745) is a famous figure in Tibetan history.

paragraphs.source_zh: 仓央嘉错（一六八三――一七四五），是西藏历史上著名的人物。出生在门隅拉沃宇松地方，从小资质灵敏，曾拜五世班禅为师，落发受戒，取法名为罗桑仁青仓央嘉错。后被迎至布达拉宫，在著名学者桑杰嘉错的直接培养下，学习天文历算、医学及文学等，对诗的造诣很深。二十五岁时，作为上层统治阶级争权夺利牺牲品的仓央嘉错，开始了自己的流浪生活。先后周游了青海、甘肃、蒙古、四川、卫藏、印度、尼泊尔等地。曾当过乞丐，送过尸体，生活极为艰苦。由于接触过广大的人民群众，有丰富的生活实践，从而写出了优美动人的《仓央嘉错情歌》。一说仓央嘉错被解往北京途中遭害，所写作品为二十五岁以前的东西。

paragraphs.source_en: Tradition says that before Tsangyang Gyatso was chosen as the Dalai Lama, he had in his home village a beautiful and intelligent beloved; the two spent their days together, farming and herding, childhood companions deeply in love. After Tsangyang Gyatso entered the Potala Palace, he wearied of the monotonous and rigid life of a Yellow Hat leader deep within the palace, and constantly longed for the colorful customs of the people and for his beautiful lover. So he often went out at night in plain clothes to meet his lover and pursue a romantic life of love. One day after a heavy snowfall, the Iron-Rod Lama rose early and discovered footprints in the snow showing that someone had gone out; following the tracks, he found that they finally led into Tsangyang Gyatso's sleeping quarters. Afterward, the Iron-Rod Lama punished Tsangyang Gyatso's personal lama with severe torture, sent men to put his lover to death, and took harsh measures to confine Tsangyang Gyatso. There are many other romantic legends of this kind, but all of them end in tragedy. At the same time, Tsangyang Gyatso was also an exceptionally gifted poet of folk song, writing many passionate and unrestrained love songs; his collection Love Songs, with its beautiful wording and simple, vivid expression, was widely circulated, sung, and recited among the people.

paragraphs.source_en: Do not blame the Living Buddha Tsangyang Gyatso for being amorous and wayward; what he desired was no different from what ordinary people desire. Although Tibetans are devout Buddhists, it is said that the Dalai Lama they feel closest to in their hearts is this very Tsangyang Gyatso, who has no spirit stupa in the Potala Palace. They revere this young lama, who was murdered by political figures at only twenty-four, because his love poems expressed their love and understanding of life.

paragraphs.source_en: A seventeenth-century Tibetan collection of love songs, by the Sixth Dalai Lama Tsangyang Gyatso (1683-?). Written by him. The author was born in the Monyul region of southern Tibet; as a child he was a herdboy, knew rural customs well, loved folk songs, and was deeply nurtured by folk literature. His father believed in Buddhism and belonged to the Nyingma school, which had a certain influence on him. At the age of fifteen, he was recognized as the reincarnated soul child of the Fifth Dalai Lama and entered the Potala Palace in Lhasa, where distinguished teachers guided him in the study of Buddhist scriptures, poetry, and calendrical calculation. Yet Tsangyang Gyatso was never able to forget secular life, and so, drawing on his own feelings, he composed a large number of poems. Later generations selected more than sixty representative works and compiled them as Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso, which were carved, printed, and handed down to the world.

paragraphs.source_zh: 17世纪藏族情歌集，第六世达赖喇嘛仓央嘉措(1683～?)著。作者生于西藏南部门隅地区，幼年当过牧童，熟悉农村风情，喜爱民歌，深受民间文学熏陶。其父信仰佛教，属宁玛派，对其有一定影响。15岁时﹐被认定为五世达赖喇嘛的转世灵童，入拉萨布达拉宫，由名师指点，学习佛教经典、诗歌和历算。但仓央嘉措始终未能忘情于世俗生活，遂以亲身感受创作了大量诗歌。后人选出60多首代表性作品，编成《仓央嘉措情歌》，刻印成书流传于世。

paragraphs.source_en: Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso is a rare and extraordinary flower in the garden of Tibetan poetry. Although the author was a religious leader, he dared to write of human inner conflicts and ideals for real life, breaking through religion's restraints on human nature, boldly challenging traditional forces, and displaying the poet's immense courage. These works are not only positive and progressive in thought and content, but also possess a high degree of artistic skill. In metrical structure, the Love Songs adopt the form of the xie-style folk song; apart from a few six-line and eight-line pieces, they are basically four lines to a poem, six syllables to each line, with a pause every two syllables, divided into three beats. That is, “four lines, six words, three pauses”: the rhythm is bright and resonant, and the verse rolls readily off the tongue.

paragraphs.source_en: The Tibetan originals of the Love Songs have been transmitted in some cases orally, in others through manuscripts, and in others by woodblock printing, which shows how widely they spread and how deeply Tibetan readers loved them. There are at least ten Chinese translations at home and abroad, and overseas there are translations in English, French, Japanese, Russian, Hindi, and other languages. Thus the Love Songs enjoy high renown not only in the history of Tibetan literature, but also in the world of poetry.

paragraphs.source_en: Tsangyang Gyatso was born in 1683 in Yusong, in the Monyul region of southern Tibet, into a peasant family that for generations had believed in Nyingma Buddhism. In 1697, Tsangyang Gyatso was chosen as the “reincarnated soul child” of the Fifth Dalai Lama; in September of that year he was escorted from southern Tibet to Lhasa, and when passing through Nagarze County, he took the Fifth Panchen Lama Lobsang Yeshe (1663-1737) as his teacher, shaved his head and received ordination, and was given the Dharma name Lobsang Rinchen Tsangyang Gyatso. On October 25 of the same year, an enthronement ceremony was held at the Potala Palace in Lhasa, and he became the Sixth Dalai Lama. Before this, Tsangyang Gyatso had lived among the people; although his family had for generations believed in Nyingma, or Red Hat, Buddhism, the rules of that school did not forbid monks to marry and have children. By contrast, the Gelug, or Yellow Hat, Buddhism to which the Dalai Lama belonged strictly forbade monks to marry, establish families, or approach women. Tsangyang Gyatso found it difficult to accept such pure rules and strict prohibitions. Not only did he fail to use religious rules to constrain his thoughts, words, and deeds; instead, from his prominent position as a religious leader and according to his own independent thought and will, he wrote many lingering and tender “love songs.”
